# Supporting check: BKT vs percentage of correct answers

**SOURCE: synthetic (generated by code with a fixed seed; not a research result)**

Seed 20261118; 3000 students per scenario, 12 answers each on one skill. The app's BKT always uses its config defaults (p_init 0.2, learn 0.15, slip 0.1, guess 0.25); mastery threshold 0.8. The BKT implementation was first checked against the OQ-11 numbers of the SPEC.

## True process per scenario

| Scenario | p_init | learn | slip | guess |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| matched | 0.2 | 0.15 | 0.1 | 0.25 |
| mismatched | 0.35 | 0.08 | 0.2 | 0.25 |
| lucky_guessing | 0.2 | 0.15 | 0.1 | 0.4 |

## Predicting the next answer (AUC, pooled over answers 2..12)

| Scenario | BKT AUC [95 % CI] | Share-correct AUC [95 % CI] | Difference BKT − share [95 % CI] |
|---|---|---|---|
| matched | 0.773 [0.767, 0.778] | 0.733 [0.725, 0.739] | +0.040 [+0.036, +0.044] |
| mismatched | 0.719 [0.712, 0.725] | 0.699 [0.692, 0.705] | +0.020 [+0.016, +0.023] |
| lucky_guessing | 0.720 [0.713, 0.726] | 0.663 [0.656, 0.670] | +0.057 [+0.052, +0.061] |

Bootstrap over students (500 resamples). Predictions are pooled over answer positions: the share divides by the number of answers so far and BKT does not, and BKT also weighs recent answers more; both contribute to the difference.

## Declaring mastery

These rules look at the stream continuously; the app gates after a node test of at least 3 questions per skill (F5-R3) with rounds, so none of these rates is the app's rate. False positive = the rule fires while the student is, in truth, still in the unknown state. Delay = answers between the student truly learning and the rule firing (only for correct declarations). Missed = truly learned within 12 answers but never declared.

| Scenario | Rule | Declared | False positives | Median delay (answers) | Missed |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| matched | BKT >= 0.80 | 91.3 % | 17.0 % | 2.0 | 3.1 % |
| matched | share correct >= 80 % (all answers, min 3) | 40.2 % | 2.5 % | 3.0 | 55.1 % |
| matched | last 3 answers all correct | 80.9 % | 4.0 % | 3.0 | 10.4 % |
| matched | 4 of the last 5 correct | 78.8 % | 2.2 % | 4.0 | 12.4 % |
| mismatched | BKT >= 0.80 | 84.0 % | 20.4 % | 2.0 | 4.6 % |
| mismatched | share correct >= 80 % (all answers, min 3) | 36.8 % | 2.7 % | 2.0 | 52.7 % |
| mismatched | last 3 answers all correct | 69.0 % | 6.3 % | 3.0 | 13.8 % |
| mismatched | 4 of the last 5 correct | 66.1 % | 3.8 % | 4.0 | 16.2 % |
| lucky_guessing | BKT >= 0.80 | 96.5 % | 31.1 % | 2.0 | 1.2 % |
| lucky_guessing | share correct >= 80 % (all answers, min 3) | 49.2 % | 10.8 % | 2.0 | 45.6 % |
| lucky_guessing | last 3 answers all correct | 86.5 % | 13.3 % | 3.0 | 6.8 % |
| lucky_guessing | 4 of the last 5 correct | 84.5 % | 9.5 % | 4.0 | 8.2 % |

## How to read this

- The generator is a BKT process; "matched" is the best case for BKT and "mismatched"/"lucky_guessing" test it with wrong parameters. A percentage rule needs no parameters, which is its advantage in real life and is not captured here. The cumulative share is a weak baseline (an early mistake is never forgotten); the window rules are the fairer simple alternatives.
- Real learners forget, vary by question and are not a two-state machine. Nothing here is evidence about real learners; it only compares the two trackers on data whose truth we know.
